title: Lead, kindly light
hook: John Henry Newman, stuck on a windless sea, writes a poem that asks for one step at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, Father Zosima, the elder in Dostoevsky's novel, who taught that each of us answers for everyone. Your line was responsible for all. Which shared problem did you pick up? Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

No wind. A sailing boat sits on flat water between Corsica and Sardinia, going nowhere. On board is an English clergyman named John Henry Newman, weak from a fever he caught in Sicily, aching to get home, and unable to move. You can't argue with a calm sea. You can't row a sailing boat home. You can only wait. So, by the story Newman himself told, he writes a short poem. It is honest about the dark, and it asks for surprisingly little. Later it was set to music and sung as a hymn. Today's word is the first word of that poem, and it is a request.
screen: `A SICK MAN WANTS TO GO HOME.`

segments.voice: Here is how the poem opens: "Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom, Lead Thou me on!" Notice what he doesn't ask for. He doesn't ask for the wind. He doesn't ask for a map. Then comes the line the whole poem leans on: "Keep Thou my feet; I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me." Turn it one way, and it's a confession. In the next verse he admits he used to be different: "I loved to choose and see my path; but now Lead Thou me on!" Here is a man who liked to plan, now stuck on a sea that won't take orders. Turn it another way, and it's very old. Newman called the poem The Pillar of the Cloud. That points back to Exodus, where the King James Bible says "the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light." Israel in the wilderness never saw the whole route either. They saw the cloud, and they followed it. Turn it a third way, and it sounds like a psalm: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet." A lamp carried at night lights the ground right in front of you, and almost nothing beyond it. Enough to walk. And a fourth way: his own life. The path Newman couldn't see took him somewhere he never planned. Years later he left the Church of England and became a Catholic, which cost him friends, and the Catholic Church later named him a saint. Anglicans and Catholics both claim parts of his story. The poem stays the same: one step, then the next.
screen: `I LOVED TO CHOOSE AND SEE MY PATH.`
then, large: `ONE STEP ENOUGH FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take just the next step. Settle, and breathe. This time, begin with the fog. Let the worries about how things turn out come to mind one at a time: next month, next year, the end of the road. As each one arrives, name it, and set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor. The distant scene. Set it down. Then look only at the ground right in front of you: the next hour. What does that hour ask of you? It may be very small. A glass of water, a reply, a rest. That's enough. If you pray, you can borrow Newman's words: lead Thou me on. If you don't, let that one small thing be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Lead. The first word of Newman's poem, a request from someone who can't see the way: go ahead of me, and I'll follow.
Your line: one step enough. Today, when the whole road looks too long, do only the next thing on it, and let that count. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Newman's poem is sung as the hymn Lead, Kindly Light in some English-speaking churches, and Christians in hard seasons sometimes pray its lines when they can't see what comes next.

fork.setup: you're on a boat that can't move, sick, far from home, with no idea when the wind will come. what do you do?
options: plan the whole journey home in detail.
write a poem asking only to be led one step at a time.
give up on getting home at all.
fork.reveal: by Newman's own account, he wrote the poem: "I do not ask to see the distant scene; one step enough for me." the man who loved to plan asked for less.
